opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, it's a pleasure to be here.

That's a question we've been thinking about quite a lot. The way we approach it is to build simple synthetic models of data that have a hierarchical, compositional structure, a bit like a grammar. You have high-level features that get expanded into lower-level ones, and those into lower-level ones still, until you reach the tokens or pixels you actually observe. The question is then: how many examples does a network need to discover that hidden structure, and in what order does it discover it?

For next-token prediction, the picture that emerges is quite intuitive. With little data, the model can only exploit very local correlations: which tokens tend to appear next to which. As you increase the training set, it can resolve correlations over longer distances, and those correlations are precisely what reveal the higher levels of the hierarchy. Tokens that play the same role, like synonyms, have the same statistical relationships with the rest of the context. Once you have enough data to measure those correlations above the sampling noise, the network can group them together and build a representation of the latent variable one level up. So you get a sequence of steps: each new level of the hierarchy is learned at a characteristic training set size, and the effective context the model uses grows with the amount of data. That gives you a natural explanation for why the test loss keeps decreasing in a staircase-like or power-law fashion.

For diffusion models, what's striking is that the same mechanism is at play, but you see it through a different lens. In diffusion you add noise and the model learns to undo it. Here too the model first captures local structure. With little data, generated samples are locally coherent: the small pieces look right, but globally they don't make sense. As you add data, coherence extends to larger and larger scales, because the model has learned the higher-level variables that tie distant parts together. So in both cases, data size sets a length scale up to which the generated output is consistent, and that length scale grows with the number of examples.

There's also an interesting connection with the noise level in diffusion. If you add a small amount of noise and denoise, you tend to change low-level details while keeping the high-level structure. If you add a lot, high-level features can flip. And there's a sort of phase transition at intermediate noise where the class or the global meaning changes, while correlations between changes become long-ranged, like near a critical point. That's a nice probe of the hierarchical representation the model has learned.

So in short, I'd say the two paradigms are less different than they appear. Both learn structure hierarchically, from local to global, and in both cases the key quantity is how much data you need to detect correlations that reveal the next level up. And that, I think, is a big part of what underlies scaling laws, and also what tells us about the limits: deep, compositional structure is learnable, but each extra level of abstraction comes at a cost in data.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly asks how many examples a network needs to discover hidden structure and explains how the amount of training data determines which levels it learns.

r002.rationale: It describes both paradigms as learning hierarchically from local structure to global structure as data increases, with each higher level learned after enough data reveals its correlations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that's a question I like, because for me the two are really two sides of the same story. The story is that natural data, whether images or language, have a hierarchical, compositional structure. So you have low-level features that combine into higher-level features, which combine into even higher-level ones, and so on. The way we think about this is with simple generative models, essentially random hierarchy models inspired by context-free grammars, where you have a latent variable at the top, it generates sub-features, and those generate sub-features, down to the tokens or the pixels. And then you can ask very precisely: as a function of the number of training examples, which of these levels of structure does a learning algorithm actually capture?

What we find is that in both cases, learning happens from the bottom up. With little data, the model learns the correlations between nearby tokens, or nearby patches of the image, which is really the lowest level of the hierarchy. And then, as you increase the data, it learns the next level, and the next one. Each level requires, roughly speaking, a number of samples that grows geometrically, and so if you look at how the loss decreases with the size of the training set, you get a staircase, or if there are many levels, something that looks like a power law. So this is a way of rationalizing the scaling laws people observe empirically: they come from resolving ever-larger, ever-deeper structures in the data.

Now, the difference between diffusion and next-token prediction is in what the model is forced to look at. In next-token prediction you have a causal structure: you predict the next token from the past, and what matters is how far back in the context the model can effectively use information. So the staircase there is really about the effective context length growing with data. For diffusion, it's a denoising problem, and there is this beautiful feature that at different noise levels, you probe different scales of the hierarchy. At small noise, you only need the local structure to denoise, and at large noise, you need the global structure, the class, the overall composition. So in diffusion, the hierarchy is not only revealed as you add data, but also as you move along the noise axis, and you can see phase transitions in the backward process where the high-level features get decided and then the lower-level ones get filled in.

But the striking thing, to me, is that the sample complexity turns out to be very similar in the two cases. In both, the number of samples you need to learn a given level is set by the number of possible features at that level times the amount of data needed to detect the relevant correlations above the noise, and that gives you a polynomial, not an exponential, in the input dimension. That's the key point: if the data were not hierarchical, it would be a curse of dimensionality. Because they are, and because deep architectures and these training objectives can exploit the hierarchy one level at a time, you escape it. So I would say the mechanism is the same, learning the grammar of the data layer by layer, and the objectives just offer slightly different windows onto that same process.

r001.rationale: The response compares the models by asking which hierarchy levels they capture as training examples increase and explicitly discusses the samples needed to learn each level.

r002.rationale: It says learning happens bottom up in both cases: nearby-token or nearby-patch correlations come first, followed by progressively higher levels as data increases.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful distinction is between the learning objective and the structure of the data. In diffusion, you learn to reconstruct data from a noisy observation, at different noise levels. In next-token prediction, you learn the distribution of the next token given the preceding ones. Neither objective explicitly tells you what the underlying structure is.

As you increase the amount of data, the question is which dependencies become learnable. Simple statistical regularities may be accessible with relatively little data, while dependencies involving many variables can require much more. So an improvement in the loss need not mean that all levels of structure are improving together.

Diffusion gives you a particularly interesting way to probe this because you can vary the noise. At low noise, local information can be sufficient to reconstruct something; at high noise, you may need broader statistical information. But I would be careful about identifying noise levels directly with levels of abstraction—that depends on the data.

For next-token prediction, the corresponding question is how much of the context the model actually uses, and which dependencies it has learned within that context. So I would compare the two by asking when particular kinds of structure become accessible as the dataset grows, rather than assuming that one learns structure and the other merely predicts. Prediction is precisely what can force the model to learn structure.

r001.rationale: It compares when different dependencies become learnable as the dataset grows, directly framing the comparison around how much training data learning structure requires.

r002.rationale: It says simple regularities may be learned with less data than dependencies involving many variables, but does not identify a shared progression from lower-level grammatical constraints to higher-level constraints in both models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is not just how the error decreases with more data, but which structures become learnable at each stage. You can get a smooth improvement in the loss while the model is acquiring quite different kinds of correlations.

For diffusion, the learning problem depends on the noise level. At low noise, you can make progress using relatively local information, because much of the input is still visible. At high noise, those details are gone, and improving the prediction requires learning broader statistical structure. So there is a natural way to probe what the model has learned at different scales.

With next-token prediction, all of these contributions are mixed into the same objective. You can improve by learning frequent, short-range correlations, but also by discovering dependencies over a much longer context. The objective does not explicitly separate those scales in the way the noise level does for diffusion.

So I would be careful about saying that one necessarily learns structure faster than the other. That depends on the data and on what you mean by structure. The useful comparison is to specify a dependency in the data and ask how many examples each method needs before it can exploit it. The overall loss alone can hide that distinction.

r001.rationale: It frames the comparison around how many examples each method needs to exploit a specified dependency, directly addressing sample complexity.

r002.rationale: It contrasts local or short-range correlations with broader or longer-context structure, but does not say that lower-level grammatical constraints are learned before higher-level constraints in both methods.
